source: IELTS Writing Band Descriptors (updated May 2023) and IELTS Writing Key Assessment Criteria, published by the IELTS partners (British Council, IDP IELTS, Cambridge University Press & Assessment): https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-band-descriptors.pdf and https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-key-assessment-criteria.pdf
note: Condensed paraphrase of the public IELTS Writing band descriptors (revised 2023) for grading prompts; not official wording.

task1.applies_to: Academic Task 1 (describe visual information) and General Training Task 1 (letter). Statements marked (Academic) or (General Training) apply only to that module; everything else applies to both.

criteria.name: Task Achievement
criteria.assesses: How fully, appropriately, accurately and relevantly the response meets the task requirements in at least 150 words. Academic: selecting key features, giving enough detail to illustrate them, reporting figures and trends accurately, comparing/contrasting by highlighting the main trends, changes or differences (not mechanical listing), appropriate format; no speculation beyond the data. General Training: stating the purpose clearly, fully covering and extending all three bullet points, letter format, and a tone kept consistently appropriate to the reader.

bands.9: Meets every requirement of the task fully and appropriately. Content lapses, if any, are extremely rare. (Academic) Key features are selected, highlighted and illustrated with complete judgement within a clear overview. (General Training) The purpose, tone and all three bullet points are handled fully and appropriately from start to finish.
bands.8: Covers all requirements of the task appropriately, relevantly and in sufficient depth. (Academic) Key features are skilfully chosen and are clearly presented, highlighted and illustrated with well-chosen data. (General Training) Every bullet point is clearly presented and appropriately illustrated or extended. Only occasional omissions or lapses in content occur.
bands.7: Covers the requirements of the task; content is relevant and accurate with at most a few omissions or lapses, and the format is appropriate. (Academic) Gives a clear overview: the data are sensibly grouped or categorised and the main trends, differences or stages are identified. (Academic) The selected key features are covered and clearly highlighted but could be illustrated or extended more fully or more appropriately. (General Training) All three bullet points are covered and clearly highlighted but could be extended or illustrated more fully; the purpose is clear and the tone is consistent and suited to the reader, with minimal lapses.
bands.6: Focuses on the requirements of the task and uses an appropriate format. (Academic) Selected key features are covered and adequately highlighted, and a relevant overview is attempted (it is there, but not clear or complete enough for band 7); information is appropriately selected and supported with figures/data. (General Training) All bullet points are covered and adequately highlighted; the purpose is generally clear, although the tone may be slightly inconsistent. Some irrelevant, inappropriate or inaccurate information may appear in details or when points are illustrated or extended. Some details may be missing or excessive, and more extension or illustration is needed.
bands.5: Generally addresses the task, though the format may be inappropriate in places. (Academic) The selected key features are not adequately covered; detail is recounted mechanically, and the description may be unsupported by any data (a limiting feature). (General Training) All bullet points are presented but at least one is inadequately covered; the purpose may be unclear at times and the tone may be variable or sometimes inappropriate. There may be a tendency to dwell on details without referring to the bigger picture (e.g. no overview). Irrelevant, inappropriate or inaccurate material in key areas detracts from the response, and main points are extended or illustrated with only limited detail.
bands.4: Attempts to address the task. (Academic) Only a few key features are selected. (General Training) Not all bullet points are presented (a limiting feature); the purpose of the letter is not clearly explained and may be confused, and the tone may be inappropriate (a limiting feature). The format may be inappropriate (a limiting feature). The key features or bullet points that do appear may be irrelevant, repetitive, inaccurate or inappropriate.
bands.3: Does not address the task requirements, possibly because the data, diagram or situation has been misunderstood. What is presented may be largely irrelevant, and the limited information given may be repeated.
bands.2: What is written has almost no connection to the task.
bands.1: The content is wholly unrelated to the task, or the response is 20 words or fewer. Copied rubric is discounted.
bands.0: Used only if the candidate did not attend or attempt the task, wrote in a language other than English throughout, or the answer is proven to be totally memorised.

criteria.name: Coherence and Cohesion
criteria.assesses: Overall organisation and logical progression; paragraphing for topic organisation; sequencing of information within and across paragraphs; flexible reference and substitution (articles, pronouns); discourse markers that signal stages and relationships between ideas.

bands.9: The message can be followed without any effort. Cohesion is so natural that it rarely draws attention to itself, and any lapses in coherence or cohesion are minimal. Paragraphs are handled skilfully.
bands.8: The message is easy to follow. Information and ideas are sequenced logically and cohesion is well managed, with only occasional lapses in coherence or cohesion. Paragraphing is sufficient and appropriate.
bands.7: Information and ideas are logically organised with a clear progression throughout; a few lapses may occur. A range of cohesive devices, including reference and substitution, is used flexibly, though with some inaccuracy or some under- or over-use (e.g. linkers that are occasionally mechanical or missing).
bands.6: Ideas are mostly organised coherently and the response progresses clearly overall. Linking devices work to some good effect, but connections within or between sentences can be faulty or mechanical (devices misused, overused or missing). Referencing and substitution may be inflexible or unclear, causing some repetition or error.
bands.5: Organisation is evident but not wholly logical, and overall progression may be lacking, although an underlying coherence remains. The relationship between ideas can be followed, but sentences are not fluently linked to each other. Cohesive devices may be limited or overused, with some inaccuracy. Inadequate or inaccurate reference and substitution may make the writing repetitive.
bands.4: Information and ideas are present but not arranged coherently, and there is no clear progression. Relationships between ideas may be unclear or inadequately marked; basic cohesive devices are used, possibly inaccurately or repetitively. Substitution and referencing are inaccurate or missing.
bands.3: No apparent logical organisation; ideas can be picked out but are hard to relate to each other. Sequencers and cohesive devices are minimal and may not signal logical relationships; referencing is hard to identify.
bands.2: Little relevant message, or the whole response may be off-topic (a limiting feature). Little evidence of control of organisational features.
bands.1: Fails to communicate any message and appears to be the work of a virtual non-writer, or the response is 20 words or fewer.
bands.0: Used only if the candidate did not attend or attempt the task, wrote in a language other than English throughout, or the answer is proven to be totally memorised.

criteria.name: Lexical Resource
criteria.assesses: Range of general and topic-specific vocabulary (including synonyms to avoid repetition); adequacy, appropriacy and precision of word choice; control of collocation, idiomatic and sophisticated phrasing; density and communicative effect of spelling and word-formation errors.

bands.9: Vocabulary is used with complete flexibility and precision within the scope of the task. A wide range of words is handled accurately and appropriately, with very natural and sophisticated control of lexical features. Slips in spelling or word formation are extremely rare and barely affect communication.
bands.8: A wide resource is used fluently and flexibly to express precise meanings within the scope of the task. Uncommon and/or idiomatic items are used skilfully where appropriate, despite occasional inaccuracies in word choice and collocation. Occasional errors in spelling or word formation have minimal impact on communication.
bands.7: The resource is sufficient to allow some flexibility and precision. The writer can use some less common and/or idiomatic items and shows awareness of style and collocation, though inappropriacies occur. There are only a few spelling or word-formation errors and they do not detract from overall clarity.
bands.6: The resource is generally adequate and appropriate for the task. Meaning is generally clear despite a rather restricted range or imprecise word choice. A writer who takes risks will show a wider range but with more inaccuracy or inappropriacy. Some spelling or word-formation errors occur but do not impede communication.
bands.5: The resource is limited but minimally adequate for the task. Simple vocabulary may be accurate, but the range allows little variation in expression. Word choice frequently lapses in appropriacy, and a lack of flexibility shows in frequent simplification and/or repetition. Spelling or word-formation errors may be noticeable and may cause the reader some difficulty.
bands.4: The resource is limited and inadequate for, or unrelated to, the task (vocabulary unrelated to the task is a limiting feature). Vocabulary is basic and may be repetitive. Lexical chunks may be used inappropriately: memorised phrases, formulaic language or language lifted from the input material. Inappropriate word choice and/or spelling or word-formation errors may impede meaning.
bands.3: The resource is inadequate, possibly because the response is significantly under length, and may depend heavily on the input material or memorised language. Control of word choice and spelling is very limited; errors predominate and may severely impede meaning.
bands.2: Extremely limited resource with few recognisable strings apart from memorised phrases; no apparent control of word formation or spelling.
bands.1: No resource apart from a few isolated words, or the response is 20 words or fewer.
bands.0: Used only if the candidate did not attend or attempt the task, wrote in a language other than English throughout, or the answer is proven to be totally memorised.

criteria.name: Grammatical Range and Accuracy
criteria.assesses: Range and appropriacy of structures (simple, compound, complex sentences); accuracy of each sentence type; density and communicative effect of grammatical errors; accurate and appropriate punctuation.

bands.9: Shows full flexibility and control across a wide range of structures (within the scope of the task). Grammar and punctuation are appropriate from start to finish; minor slips are extremely rare and barely affect communication.
bands.8: Handles a wide range of structures (within the scope of the task) flexibly and accurately. The majority of sentences contain no errors and punctuation is well handled. Occasional slips or inappropriacies are non-systematic and barely affect communication.
bands.7: Uses a variety of complex sentence types with some flexibility and accuracy. Control of grammar and punctuation is generally good, and error-free sentences are frequent. A few grammatical errors may remain, but they never block understanding.
bands.6: A mix of simple and complex sentence forms is used, but flexibility is limited. The more complex structures are noticeably less accurate than the simple ones. Grammar and punctuation errors occur but rarely impede communication.
bands.5: The range of structures is limited and rather repetitive. Complex sentences are attempted but tend to be faulty; accuracy is greatest in simple sentences. Grammatical errors may be frequent and cause the reader some difficulty, and punctuation may be faulty.
bands.4: Very few structure types appear: mostly simple sentences, with subordinate clauses rare (a limiting feature). Some forms are correct, but grammar errors are frequent and can obscure meaning, and punctuation is often wrong or missing.
bands.3: Sentence forms are attempted, but grammar and punctuation errors predominate (except in memorised phrases or language copied from the input), so most meaning does not come through. The response may be too short to show control of sentence forms (a limiting feature).
bands.2: Little or no evidence of sentence forms apart from memorised phrases.
bands.1: No rateable language, or the response is 20 words or fewer.
bands.0: Used only if the candidate did not attend or attempt the task, wrote in a language other than English throughout, or the answer is proven to be totally memorised.

task2.applies_to: Academic and General Training Task 2 (essay). The descriptors are identical for both modules.

criteria.name: Task Response
criteria.assesses: Formulating and developing a position on the given prompt (question or statement) in at least 250 words: how fully every part of the prompt is answered; how well main ideas are extended and supported with evidence/examples (which may come from the writer's own experience); relevance; how clearly the writer opens, establishes a position and draws conclusions; appropriacy of the essay format.

bands.9: Addresses the prompt appropriately and explores it in depth. A clear, fully developed position answers the question(s) directly. Ideas are relevant, thoroughly extended and well supported, and lapses in content or support are extremely rare.
bands.8: Addresses the prompt appropriately and sufficiently. A clear, well-developed position is presented in response to the question(s). Ideas are relevant and well extended and supported, with only occasional omissions or lapses in content.
bands.7: Deals appropriately with the main parts of the prompt and presents a clear, developed position. Main ideas are extended and supported, although the writer may over-generalise or the supporting material may lack focus and precision.
bands.6: Addresses the main parts of the prompt, though some are covered more fully than others; the format is appropriate. A position directly relevant to the prompt is presented, but the conclusions drawn may be unclear, unjustified or repetitive. Main ideas are relevant, but some are underdeveloped or unclear, and some supporting arguments or evidence may be less relevant or inadequate.
bands.5: The main parts of the prompt are addressed incompletely (a limiting feature: e.g. one question of a two-part prompt, or the requested opinion, is missing); the format may be inappropriate in places. The writer expresses a position, but its development is not always clear. Some main ideas are offered but they are limited and insufficiently developed and/or mixed with irrelevant detail, and there may be some repetition.
bands.4: The prompt is tackled only minimally, or the answer is tangential, possibly because the prompt was misunderstood; the format may be inappropriate (a limiting feature). A position can be found only by reading carefully. Main ideas are hard to identify, and those that can be identified may lack relevance, clarity or support. Large parts of the response may be repetitive.
bands.3: Fails to deal adequately with any part of the prompt, or misreads it. There is no identifiable relevant position and little direct answer to the question(s); ideas are few and may be irrelevant or undeveloped.
bands.2: Almost nothing relates to the prompt and no position is identifiable; at most one or two ideas are glimpsed, without development.
bands.1: The content is wholly unrelated to the prompt, or the response is 20 words or fewer. Copied rubric is discounted.
bands.0: Used only if the candidate did not attend or attempt the task, wrote in a language other than English throughout, or the answer is proven to be totally memorised.

criteria.name: Coherence and Cohesion

bands.9: The message can be followed without any effort. Cohesion is so natural that it rarely draws attention to itself, and any lapses in coherence or cohesion are minimal. Paragraphs are handled skilfully.
bands.8: The message is easy to follow. Information and ideas are sequenced logically and cohesion is well managed, with only occasional lapses. Paragraphing is sufficient and appropriate.
bands.7: Information and ideas are logically organised with a clear progression throughout; any lapses are minor. A range of cohesive devices, including reference and substitution, is used flexibly, though with some inaccuracy or some under- or over-use. Paragraphing generally supports overall coherence, and ideas within each paragraph are generally sequenced logically.
bands.6: Ideas are mostly organised coherently and the response progresses clearly overall. bands.4: Information and ideas are present but not arranged coherently, and there is no clear progression. Relationships between ideas may be unclear or inadequately marked; basic cohesive devices are used, possibly inaccurately or repetitively. Substitution and referencing are inaccurate or missing. There may be no paragraphing and/or paragraphs may lack a clear main topic.
bands.3: No apparent logical organisation; ideas can be picked out but are hard to relate to each other. Sequencers and cohesive devices are minimal and may not signal logical relationships; referencing is hard to identify; any attempt at paragraphing is unhelpful.
bands.2: Little relevant message, or the whole response may be off-topic (a limiting feature). Little evidence of control of organisational features.
bands.1: Fails to communicate any message and appears to be the work of a virtual non-writer, or the response is 20 words or fewer.
bands.0: Used only if the candidate did not attend or attempt the task, wrote in a language other than English throughout, or the answer is proven to be totally memorised.

examiner_notes: Best-fit rule: award a criterion the highest band whose positive features the script FULLY fits. If it shows most but not all of the band-7 features, it is a 6. Rate each of the four criteria independently as a whole band (0–9); do not let one weak criterion drag down the others.

Limiting features (shown in bold in the official descriptors) cap a rating whatever the other strengths. Task 1: (Academic) no data supporting the description → TA max 5; (GT) a bullet point not presented → TA max 4; (GT) inappropriate tone → TA max 4; inappropriate format (e.g. notes, bullet points, an essay instead of a letter) → TA max 4. Task 2: main parts of the prompt incompletely addressed → TR max 5; inappropriate format → TR max 4; paragraphing inadequate or missing → CC max 5. Both tasks: vocabulary unrelated to the task → LR max 4; subordinate clauses rare and simple sentences predominating → GRA max 4; too short to show control of sentence forms → GRA max 3; the entire response off-topic → CC max 2; content wholly unrelated → TA/TR 1; 20 words or fewer → band 1 on every criterion; proof of a totally memorised answer → 0.

Weighting: each task is marked independently. Within a task the four criteria are weighted equally (task band = mean of the four criterion bands). Task 2 counts twice as much as Task 1, so Writing ≈ (Task 1 band + 2 × Task 2 band) / 3.

Rounding: IELTS does not publish how the weighted Writing mean is rounded. The published rule for the OVERALL band (the mean of Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking) is to round to the nearest half band, with .25 rounded up to the next half band and .75 up to the next whole band (6.25 → 6.5; 6.75 → 7.0; 6.1 → 6.0). App convention (see data/descriptors/score-conversion.json, used by BandCalculator): task band = mean of the four criteria rounded DOWN to the nearest half band; Writing band = (Task 1 + 2 × Task 2) / 3 rounded to the nearest half band. The round-down step is deliberately conservative, not official. In feedback, show every criterion band and both task bands.

Under-length (Task 1 < 150 words, Task 2 < 250 words): the minimum length is part of the task requirement (TA/TR are judged on meeting it 'using a minimum of 150/250 words'). Too little text also gives too little evidence for higher LR, GRA and CC bands; LR band 3 and GRA band 3 explicitly mention significantly under-length responses. No fixed deduction is published. App calibration (unofficial): a response a little short (≥ ~90% of the minimum) is judged normally but flagged; a clearly short one (~66–90%) rarely deserves TA/TR above 5 because development and coverage suffer; a severely short one (< ~66%) usually cannot get above 4 on TA/TR, and LR/GRA are limited by lack of evidence. 20 words or fewer = band 1. Writing more than the minimum is never penalised, but a very long Task 1 costs time for Task 2.

Word count: count the candidate's own words only. Words copied from the prompt are discounted and do not count towards the minimum. Numbers written as figures are usually counted as words. Titles are not needed.

Copying the prompt: copied rubric earns no credit for LR or GRA and does not count towards length. The introduction should paraphrase the task (e.g. 'The line graph illustrates…'), not reproduce it. Reusing essential topic words (e.g. 'public transport') is fine, but lifting whole clauses is not. Heavy dependence on input language is itself a band 3–4 LR/GRA feature.

Memorised or formulaic language: prepared templates, all-purpose phrases and memorised paragraphs (e.g. 'In this day and age, X is a hotly debated topic') show no real lexical control. They count against LR where they do not fit (band 4: inappropriate use of memorised phrases/formulaic language). Grammar inside memorised chunks is not evidence of control (GRA 2–3 carve-outs). An answer proven to be wholly memorised scores 0. A memorised essay on a neighbouring topic is off-topic or tangential: TR 1–4 depending on how little of it relates to the prompt.

Off-topic and tangential answers: writing about a wider or different topic than the one asked (e.g. 'computers in general' when the prompt is about one specific aspect of them) is penalised under TA/TR. Tangential → TR 4; barely related → 2; wholly unrelated → 1. Vocabulary unrelated to the task limits LR to 4 and an entirely off-topic response limits CC to 2.

Bullet points and notes: both tasks must be written as full, connected prose. Bullet points or note form in ANY part of the response is penalised: inappropriate format under TA/TR (a band-4 limiting feature when the format is inappropriate overall; 'inappropriate in places' is a band-5 feature), and it also weakens CC. GT letters must not copy the three bullet points as headings. Plagiarised (copied) text is severely penalised.

Task 1 Academic overview: this is the main difference between TA bands 5, 6 and 7. Band 7 needs a clear overview (the data grouped, with the main trends/differences/stages identified). Band 6 needs at least an attempted, relevant overview. No overview, or a mechanical run through the figures ('tendency to focus on details'), is band 5 at best. An overview may come right after the introduction or at the end, but it must summarise and not repeat detail. Report figures accurately with units. Select key features rather than listing every number, and compare where relevant. Do not add causes, speculation or personal opinion beyond the data: this is an information-transfer task. Process diagrams: the overview gives the number or type of stages and the start and end points (and whether the process is a cycle). Maps: the overview gives the overall nature of the changes.

Task 1 GT letter, purpose and tone: the purpose (complaint, request, apology, invitation, thanks, etc.) should be clear in the opening lines (band 7 'clear purpose'; 6 'generally clear'; 5 'unclear at times'; 4 'not clearly explained'). All three bullet points must be covered and extended with relevant detail; one missing bullet caps TA at 4, and one presented but thin is band 5. Tone must suit the recipient and relationship and stay consistent: minor slips = 6, variable = 5, generally inappropriate (e.g. slangy to a company manager, stiffly formal to a close friend) = 4. Letter format means a salutation, paragraphs and a suitable closing and signature; addresses are not required.

Task 2 position rules: when the prompt asks for the writer's view ('To what extent do you agree or disagree?', 'Discuss both views and give your own opinion', 'Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?'), a clear position is needed. It should normally be stated in the introduction, kept consistent through the body and confirmed in the conclusion; a position that changes or contradicts itself is at most band 6 ('conclusions unclear/unjustified'). A discussion prompt needs BOTH views discussed plus an opinion. A two-part (double-question) prompt needs BOTH questions answered. A problem–solution prompt needs both problems/causes and solutions. Leaving out a required part = 'main parts incompletely addressed' → TR max 5. Balanced partial agreement is fine if it is clearly stated.

Task 2 development: bands 7+ need main ideas that are extended (explained, with a consequence or example) and supported, not just listed. Band 7 allows some over-generalisation. Band 6 is typical when ideas are relevant but some are thin, unclear or backed with weak examples. Examples may come from personal experience. Opinions are not judged for correctness, only for relevance, development and support.

Cohesion traps: mechanical linking (a linker opening almost every sentence: Firstly / Moreover / Furthermore / In addition), linkers used with the wrong meaning, and repetition from weak referencing (repeating the noun instead of using it/this/they/such) are typical band 5–6 features. Band 7 allows some over- or under-use as long as the devices are used flexibly. Task 1 descriptors mention paragraphing only at bands 8–9, but grouping the data logically into paragraphs supports progression at every band. In Task 2, missing or illogical paragraphing is penalised directly (band 5 cap if missing).

Lexis and grammar evidence: band 7 LR needs some less common items with awareness of style and collocation; forced 'advanced' words and wrong collocations are inappropriacies, not credit. Band 7 GRA needs a variety of complex structures and frequent error-free sentences; band 8 needs a majority of error-free sentences. Judge error density and whether errors impede meaning. British and American spellings are both acceptable. Punctuation is assessed under GRA.

Register: both tasks call for academic or semi-formal/neutral style, except GT Task 1, whose register depends on the recipient (personal, semi-formal or formal). Contractions, slang and emotive or conversational style in an essay are LR/TR appropriacy issues, not grammar errors.
